newsitem.title: USA: Oregon staff sets Enron merger terms.
newsitem.headline: Oregon staff sets Enron merger terms.

text.p: In a preliminary review, the staff of the Oregon Public Utilities Commission said Thursday Enron Corp and Portland General Electric Co need to meet several conditions before their merger should be approved.
The staff recommended a $47.5 million rate cut for Portland General customers over four years, followed by an $11.2 million rate reduction that would reamin until the utility's next rate case.

The staff also recommended standards for minimum service quality, restrictions to ensure the financial viability of the utility, various reporting requirements, cost-shifting protections and competitive protections.
In all, the staff set 23 conditions.
Houston-based Enron and Portland General announced in July plans to merge via a tax-free stock-for-stock deal valued near $2.1 billion.
Most analysts praised the move as part of a growing trend to capitalize on deregulation of electric utilities and "convergence" of energy markets.
But it also raised concerns among some industry participants about market dominance and fair competition.
In response, the companies have already committed to submitting a plan to open Portland General's service territory to other competitors within 60 days of their merger.
They have also proposed separating Portland General's generating facilities from its transmission and distribution system.
Last week several environmental and public interest groups agreed to support the merger in return for commitments by the merged company to various environmental and pro-competition initiatives.
But the merger is still opposed by other stakeholders, including several western utilities with concerns about market power and cost-shifting.
Conferences on the hearing will be held at the commission in Salem on January 22-24.
The commission staff is expected to present a final recommendation on the merger by January 31 and the commission is scheduled to announce its decision March 17.
The deal must also be approved by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.
